conclusion.original: Integrate the squared value of each coordinate over time and add the coordinate energies. The difference between the two random energies is integrable, and its mean absolute value is controlled by the product-space L² norms of the coordinatewise sums and differences. Formula: \begin{gathered} E(f)(\omega)=\sum_{j\in J}\int_0^T f_j(t,\omega)^2\,dt,\\ \int|E(\eta)-E(\xi)|\,d\mu\le\sum_{j\in J}\|\eta_j+\xi_j\|_{L^2(\Omega\times[0,T],\,\mu\otimes dt)}\|\eta_j-\xi_j\|_{L^2(\Omega\times[0,T],\,\mu\otimes dt)}.\end{gathered}
conclusion.reconstructed: Put E_eta(omega)=∑_j∫ eta_j(t,omega)² d lambda_T(t), and similarly E_xi. Then E_eta-E_xi is mu-integrable and ∫|E_eta-E_xi| dmu ≤ ∑_j ||eta_j+xi_j||_2 ||eta_j-xi_j||_2. The added and subtracted integrands have exactly the pointwise sums and differences as process fields. Here ||a||_2 is the norm of the L²(mu⊗lambda_T) equivalence class of (omega,t)↦a(t,omega), since toLp is exactly MemLp.toLp of that process function.
